# 20 Backend Security

Part of [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/Backend from First Principles|Backend from First Principles]] · Previous: [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/19 Graceful Shutdown/19 Graceful Shutdown|19 Graceful Shutdown]] · Next: [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/21.1 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 1/21.1 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 1|21.1 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 1]]

Security mistakes can be **financially destructive** for a business: lost data, lost trust, lost money. This lesson does not try to teach every security technique. Its goal is to build a **security mindset**: a healthy paranoia about the code you write, so that you always ask *"what could go wrong here?"*. It covers injection attacks, authentication, authorization, XSS, CSRF and common misconfigurations, and ends with a mental model that works in any language or framework.

---

## Contents

- [[#1. Scope: which kind of security?|1. Scope: which kind of security?]]
- [[#2. Think like an attacker|2. Think like an attacker]]
- [[#3. Injection: your app speaks many languages|3. Injection: your app speaks many languages]]
- [[#4. SQL injection|4. SQL injection]]
- [[#5. Fixing SQL injection: parameterized queries|5. Fixing SQL injection: parameterized queries]]
- [[#6. NoSQL injection|6. NoSQL injection]]
- [[#7. Command injection|7. Command injection]]
- [[#8. The injection mental model|8. The injection mental model]]
- [[#9. Authentication: consider an auth provider|9. Authentication: consider an auth provider]]
- [[#10. Storing passwords|10. Storing passwords]]
- [[#11. Sessions and cookie flags|11. Sessions and cookie flags]]
- [[#12. JWTs and their trade-offs|12. JWTs and their trade-offs]]
- [[#13. Rate limiting authentication|13. Rate limiting authentication]]

- [[#17. Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)|17. Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)]]

- [[#19. Boundaries, assumptions and defense in depth|19. Boundaries, assumptions and defense in depth]]
- [[#20. Where to learn more|20. Where to learn more]]

---

## 1. Scope: which kind of security?

Security is a huge field. It can mean:

| Area                 | Concerned with                                                                             |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Browser security** | HTML, cookies, local storage, and other places in the browser where vulnerabilities appear |
| **Network security** | The transport layer: HTTP vs HTTPS, encryption                                             |
| **Server security**  | The **operating system** your app runs on                                                  |
| **Backend security** | Vulnerabilities caused by **your application's code**                                      |

This lesson focuses on **backend security**, touching the browser where backend decisions (cookies, headers) matter.

### The goal is a mindset

- No application is ever **truly** secure. Languages, libraries and technology keep changing, so new vulnerabilities keep appearing. You still try your best.
- The aim, as in [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/08 Authentication and Authorization/08 Authentication and Authorization|lesson 08]], is to make you **paranoid** about your code, so security is always in the back of your mind.
- If a specific threat isn't covered here, the mindset still applies.

---

## 2. Think like an attacker

An **attacker** is anyone who wants to harm your application. Attackers don't care what language, framework or library you used. They ask one question:

> **Where did the developer make an assumption?**

Every vulnerability in this lesson comes down to an assumption, such as:

- the input from the user/frontend will be **clean**,
- the user is **who they say they are**,
- the request is coming from **our own frontend**,
- nobody will open the browser's **network tab**, look at the API calls, and **change the parameters**.

These assumptions feel reasonable under deadlines (especially in startups), because you think in the **happy path**: users fill forms correctly, click the right buttons and navigate the way you intended.

Attackers don't use your app the way you intended. They **poke at every boundary**, try to break every input, and look for every assumption.

The habit to build: every time you write code, ask **"what could go wrong here, security-wise?"**

---

## 3. Injection: your app speaks many languages

**Injection attacks** have existed for decades and are still common. They all share one root cause.

A backend talks to many systems, each in its own **language**:

| Talking to | Language |
|---|---|
| Database | **SQL** |
| Browser (if you serve pages/assets) | **HTML, CSS, JavaScript** |
| Operating system | **Shell** commands and system calls |
| … | LDAP, XML, and others, depending on the system |

Each language has its own **grammar**, its own **special characters**, and its own way of **separating commands from data**.

Vulnerabilities appear when **input written in one context crosses into another language's context**. A character that is harmless data to the user can be a **special command** in SQL, HTML or the shell. SQL injection and XSS are examples.

---

## 4. SQL injection

### The setup

A simple login page: email + password → server → database. The server looks up the user by email and checks the password.

Suppose the developer builds the query by **string concatenation**, dropping the user's input straight into a template:

```sql
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '<user input goes here>';
```

### The happy path

The user types `alice@gmail.com`:

```sql
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'alice@gmail.com';
```

The database finds Alice and the login proceeds.

### The attack

The attacker types this into the email field:

```text
' OR '1'='1' --
```

After concatenation the query becomes:

```sql
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '' OR '1'='1' --';
```

Reading it piece by piece:

1. The attacker's first `'` **closes** the opening quote the server added. So the first condition is `email = ''`, which is false for every row.
2. `OR '1'='1'` compares the string "1" with the string "1". That is **always true**.
3. `--` starts an **SQL comment**, so the leftover `'` from the template is ignored. Without it, the extra quote would cause a syntax error.
4. `false OR true` is **true for every row**, so the `WHERE` clause effectively disappears. The query is the same as `SELECT * FROM users;`.

### Observed in the demo

In a database client (TablePlus), a `users` table was created with `name` and `email` (text) columns and two rows: Alice and Bob.

- The happy-path query returned **only Alice's row**.
- The malicious query returned **both rows**, every user and their email, even though no real email was given.

In production, a users table usually holds much more: password hashes, addresses, phone numbers and other sensitive data.

### Worse: destroying data

The attacker could instead type:

```text
'; DROP TABLE users; --
```

which turns into:

```sql
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ''; DROP TABLE users; --';
```

The `;` ends the first statement, and the second one **deletes the whole users table**.

Observed: when this was pasted into TablePlus, the first statement returned an empty result and the **table was not dropped**. The second statement did not run. Many modern database drivers refuse to run several statements in one call, precisely because SQL injection is such an old attack. An older or less careful driver might run it.

Skilled attackers can go further:

- **`UNION`** statements to pull data from other tables (e.g. payment information),
- database-specific functions to **read files** from the server,
- in some configurations, **running OS commands** through the database.

### Least-privilege database users

A second line of defense: the database user your application connects with should only have permission for **DML** (Data Manipulation Language: `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`), not **DDL** (Data Definition Language: `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`). Then even a successful injection can't drop tables.

### Why it works: code vs data

SQL gives special meaning to certain characters and words:

| Symbol / keyword | Meaning in SQL |
|---|---|
| `'` | Starts and ends a string |
| `;` | Ends one statement; the next one begins |
| `--` | Rest of the line is a comment |
| `OR`, `DROP`, `WHERE`, … | Keywords with specific meaning |

Concatenating user input into SQL means **trusting that the input contains none of these**, which you can never guarantee. Even an innocent user might type a `'`.

The essence of every injection attack: **data gets treated as code**.

---

## 5. Fixing SQL injection: parameterized queries

The fix is **parameterized queries**, also called **prepared statements**. They **separate the query from the data**. (See also [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/12 Databases with Postgres/12 Databases with Postgres#13. Parameterized queries and SQL injection|lesson 12]].)

```js
// Illustrative; the exact syntax depends on your driver or ORM
const statement = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1";
const result = await db.query(statement, [userInput]);
```

Instead of one mashed-together string, the database receives **two separate things**:

1. **The statement**: the fixed part you wrote (tables, conditions, operations). It contains **no user data**. `$1` is a **parameter**, an empty slot to be filled later.
2. **The values**: the runtime data, e.g. the email from the request, which fills the slots.

Because the database fills the slot itself, whatever goes into it is treated **purely as data**, as a plain string. If the attacker sends `' OR '1'='1' --`, the database searches for a user whose email is literally that string. It finds **no rows** and does no harm.

Notes:

- Your **validation layer** should already reject that input, since it isn't an email (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/09 Validations and Transformations/09 Validations and Transformations|lesson 09]]). Parameterized queries protect you even when validation is weak.
- Every modern database driver supports parameterized queries, and **ORMs use them by default**. Today you're only vulnerable if you deliberately build raw SQL strings yourself.

---

## 6. NoSQL injection

Using MongoDB or another document database doesn't make you immune.

MongoDB queries are **JSON-like objects**, and they can contain **operators**, written as keys that start with `$`:

| Operator | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `$ne` | not equal |
| `$gt` | greater than |
| `$exists` | field exists |

A normal query:

```js
db.users.find({ email: "alice@gmail.com" });
```

If your app passes the user's JSON **directly** into the query, the attacker controls not just the *value* but the *structure*:

```json
{ "email": { "$ne": "" } }
```

That means "email is not empty", which matches every user. Never pass raw user objects into queries; validate their shape and types first.

---

## 7. Command injection

**Command injection** works like SQL injection, but the target is the **operating system**: a system command or a command-line tool your backend runs.

### Example

Users upload images and your backend resizes or compresses them by calling a CLI tool such as **FFmpeg**, a popular image and video processing tool. The user is allowed to choose the output file name, and you insert it straight into a shell command:

```bash
ffmpeg -i input.jpg -vf scale=220:120 <user file name>
```

A genuine user gives `output.jpg`. An attacker gives:

```text
output.jpg; rm -rf /
```

The shell sees `;`, finishes the FFmpeg command, then runs `rm -rf /`, which tries to **delete the entire filesystem**.

Attackers can also use other shell special characters:

- **pipes** (`|`) to send output into another command,
- **`&`** to run commands in the background, e.g. leaving spyware running.

Each shell (bash, zsh, fish) has its own special characters and escape sequences, which leaves plenty of room for creative exploits.

### The fix: separate the command from its arguments

Use the functions your language provides that take the **program** and its **arguments as a list**, and pass them **directly to the process without a shell**:

```js
// Illustrative (Node.js): no shell, so arguments are only data
import { execFile } from "node:child_process";
execFile("ffmpeg", ["-i", "input.jpg", "-vf", "scale=220:120", outputName]);
```

Go (`exec.Command`), Python (`subprocess.run([...])` without `shell=True`) and others work the same way. Since no shell interprets the input, `;` is just a character in a file name.

---

## 8. The injection mental model

Whenever user input travels into **another system's language** (SQL, NoSQL, shell, HTML, LDAP, XML, …):

- make sure it is treated **purely as data**, never as something that can be executed or interpreted,
- use APIs that **separate structure from data**:
  - **parameterized queries** for databases,
  - **argument arrays** for OS commands,
- **never** build these strings by concatenation or template strings that mix user input with control syntax.

> **Rule of thumb:** whenever you're building a string that another system will interpret, and it contains user input, stop and look for a parameterized alternative. One almost always exists.

---

## 9. Authentication: consider an auth provider

**Authentication** verifies **who the user is**: which row in your users table matches the person making the request. Get it wrong and attackers can **impersonate users**, read their private data, act on their behalf, or steal money. **Account takeovers** happen in the real world every day.

### Advice: use an auth provider if you can

If you have the budget and approval, use an **authentication provider** (e.g. **Clerk**) instead of building the whole flow yourself, at least in production. This means the whole flow, not just "don't write your own cryptography".

A simple flow (sign a JWT, store it in a cookie, verify it) is easy, and isn't where most risk lies. A **production** auth system is much more:

- **Stateful sessions**: track every device a user is logged into, and let the user (or you) **revoke** all sessions instantly. This involves databases, caches like Redis, where to store permissions, timeouts and revocation logic.
- **Social login** ("Sign in with Google / GitHub / Twitter"): OAuth flows on both backend and frontend, with smooth redirects.
- **Account linking**: if someone signed up with `email + password` and later clicks "Sign in with Google" with the **same email**, they must be recognised as the **same user**, not a new one.
- …and many more edge cases that take developers **weeks**. Cutting corners hurts either **security** or **user experience**.

Why a provider is worth it:

- It saves a lot of **time** and developer **salary**.
- Providers are **security companies** with dedicated teams working on it full-time. They handle edge cases you won't think of and respond quickly to new attacks.
- Many offer extras like **RBAC** (role-based access control) and advanced security features.

Costs grow with your user count, and providers can have their own UX issues or vulnerabilities. When the bill reaches, say, **$10,000–20,000** at thousands or millions of users, you'll likely have the revenue and team to **migrate to your own system**. When starting out, a provider is recommended.

**Even with a provider, you must understand how authentication works**: how to configure it, what can go wrong, and how to integrate it securely. The rest of this section is about that.

---

## 10. Storing passwords

Even with an auth service, most developers deal with passwords at some point. How should the backend store a password so it can check it at login?

### Attempt 1: plain text ❌

Store exactly what the user typed (`12345`) in a text column, and compare it at login. Simple, and badly wrong:

1. **Databases get breached constantly**, at companies of every size, for many reasons: a vengeful insider, a breached third-party service, and so on.
2. **Password reuse.** More than **70%** of users reuse the same email/password combination across sites; few use password managers. A leaked plain-text password lets attackers log in to that user's **other accounts** (payment, shopping, social media). This is called **credential stuffing**. Users usually don't even know a breach happened.
3. **Insiders.** Every developer, database administrator, contractor or freelancer with database access can read every user's password.

### Attempt 2: hashing

A **hash function** has three key properties:

1. **Fixed-length output**: any input, from 1 to hundreds of characters, produces output of the same fixed length.
2. **Deterministic**: the same input always gives the same output.
3. **One-way**: you can't recover the input from the output with today's computing power.

So instead of `12345`, you store `hash("12345")`, e.g. using **bcrypt**. At login you hash the submitted password and compare it with the stored hash. If they match, the password is right.

If the database leaks, attackers get **hashes**, not passwords. Safe? Not yet.

### The problem: precomputed tables

Attackers know hashing is standard. They build huge **precomputed tables** mapping **common passwords → their hashes** for popular algorithms (often called **rainbow tables**):

| Password | Hash |
|---|---|
| `12345` | `$2b…` |
| `password` | `…` |
| `password@123` | `…` |

Because hashing is deterministic, they can **look up** each leaked hash. Any user with a common password gets a match, and the attacker recovers it.

### Attempt 3: salting

A **salt** is a **random string generated for each user** using a **cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator** (CSPRNG), e.g. from OpenSSL. It is stored with the user's row.

```text
stored_hash = hash(password + salt)
```

Now two users with the password `12345` get **different** hashes, and none of them match the attacker's precomputed table. A lookup finds **zero results**.

> [!note] In practice
> Modern password-hashing libraries (bcrypt, Argon2id) **generate the salt for you** and embed it inside the stored hash string, so you usually don't need a separate salt column.

### The remaining problem: brute force on GPUs

Modern **GPUs** are extremely fast at computing hashes: a single GPU can compute **billions of SHA-256 hashes per second**, and cloud providers rent GPUs cheaply.

With a leaked database, attackers can do **offline brute forcing**: for each user, take the salt, hash candidate passwords with it, and compare. At billions per second they can try every password up to about 8 characters, every common pattern and every word with common substitutions **within days**.

### Attempt 4: slow hashing functions ✅

That's why **general-purpose hashes** like **MD5** and **SHA-256** (used e.g. to check file integrity after a download) are **not used for passwords**. They are too fast.

Use **slow, password-specific** hashing functions instead:

| Algorithm | Notes |
|---|---|
| **bcrypt** | The long-time default for web apps |
| **scrypt** | Another slow hash |
| **Argon2id** | The current recommended standard |

They have a **cost factor** (also called **work factor**) that controls how slow they are. You choose it based on your system's capacity, e.g. 5 ms or 100 ms or more per hash.

The trade-off is lopsided in your favour:

- A genuine user logging in with a hash that takes about **400 ms** barely notices; a 400–600 ms login feels normal.
- An attacker drops from **billions** of guesses per second to **a handful**. Cracking goes from days to **decades or centuries**.

> [!tip] Further reading
> **Lucia** started as an authentication library and is now a guide to implementing authentication yourself following industry practices. It's a good resource for understanding secure authentication.

---

## 11. Sessions and cookie flags

After a user proves their identity, you can't make them type their password on every request. You need to **remember** that they're authenticated. That's what **sessions** are for (background in [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/08 Authentication and Authorization/08 Authentication and Authorization#3. Three building blocks: sessions, JWTs, cookies|lesson 08]]).

### What the server does on successful login

1. **Generates a random session ID**: long (**128–256 bits**) and produced by a **CSPRNG**. If an attacker could guess session IDs, they could **hijack** anyone's session. With 128 random bits there are about 3.4 × 10³⁸ possibilities, so guessing is practically impossible.
2. **Stores the session ID** with metadata, in **Redis** (fast) or the main database (PostgreSQL, MySQL):
   - **which user** it belongs to,
   - **created at** and **expires at** (e.g. 7 days), for timeouts and revocation,
   - **IP address**, to show the user where they signed in from,
   - **user agent**, a request header saying which browser and device (Chrome, Firefox, Android, iPhone…) is being used.
3. **Sends the session ID to the browser** to be stored in a **cookie**.

On every later request the browser sends the cookie back automatically. The server extracts the session ID, looks it up in Redis or the database, finds the user, and knows who is making the request.

JWTs work differently (they are stateless; see section 12), but the idea of identifying the authenticated user on each request is the same.

### Cookie flags to use in production

#### `HttpOnly`

JavaScript running on the page **cannot read** the cookie.

- If your site has an **XSS** vulnerability (section 16), malicious JavaScript can read **local storage** and any cookie that isn't HttpOnly.
- So **don't store session IDs or JWTs in local storage**, and always set `HttpOnly` on cookies that hold them.

#### `Secure`

The browser only sends the cookie over **HTTPS**, never plain HTTP.

- HTTP traffic can be **intercepted**: on public Wi-Fi in cafés, by malicious ISPs, by a compromised router, or by anyone watching traffic with a tool like **Wireshark**.
- HTTPS traffic is **encrypted**, so even an observer can't read it. (See [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/05 HTTP for Backend Engineers/05 HTTP for Backend Engineers#14. SSL, TLS, and HTTPS|lesson 05]].)

#### `SameSite`

Controls whether the cookie is sent on **cross-site** requests, i.e. requests triggered from a different site.

| Value | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `Strict` | Sent **only** on requests that start from your own site. Even clicking a link to your site from another site won't include it. |
| `Lax` | Also sent on **top-level navigation** (following a link to your site), but **not** on cross-site requests from images, iframes or forms posting from other sites. |
| `None` | Sent on **all** requests. Requires `Secure`. |

For session cookies, prefer **`Strict`**, use **`Lax`** if needed, and **never `None`**. This is what blocks **CSRF** (section 17).

```http
Set-Cookie: session_id=k3J9…; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict; Path=/; Max-Age=604800
```

*(Illustrative header.)*

---

## 12. JWTs and their trade-offs

### Sessions vs JWTs

| | Sessions (stateful) | JWTs (stateless) |
|---|---|---|
| Where session data lives | **Server** (DB/Redis); the client only holds the ID | **In the token** the client holds |
| Server storage needed per request | Yes, a lookup | No, just verify the signature |

### Why the client can't simply lie

If the client tells the server who the user is, couldn't it just say "I'm user B"? No, because of how a JWT is built. A JWT (the example on **jwt.io**) has **three parts**:

```text
header.payload.signature
```

1. **Header**: describes the token, e.g. which **algorithm** was used.
2. **Payload**: the **claims**, key–value pieces of information:
   - `sub` (**subject**): the user's ID in your system (e.g. a UUID),
   - `iat` (**issued at**): when the token was created, which your server can use to decide whether it has expired (the standard `exp` claim stores an explicit expiry time),
   - **custom claims**, e.g. `name`, `admin: true`.
3. **Signature**: created by **signing the header + payload with a secret key**, a random, cryptographically secure string kept in the server's environment variables (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/17 Configuration Management/17 Configuration Management#6. Security|lesson 17]]).

### The flow

1. The user logs in; the password is checked with the same hashing and salting as before.
2. The server creates a JWT with the user ID and other claims, **signs** it with the secret, and sends it to the client.
3. The client stores it (in memory, local storage or a cookie) and sends it back on every request, typically in the **`Authorization` header**.
4. The server calls the library's **verify** function with the secret. If the signature is valid, the payload **hasn't been tampered with** and can be trusted.

Advantage: **no database or Redis lookup** per request, which makes **scaling** easier.

### Observed: tampering breaks the signature

The payload is only **Base64-encoded** (not encrypted). Decoding it shows the full JSON: user ID, name, admin flag, issued-at.

In the demo, the name "John Doe" in the payload was changed to "John Do", re-encoded in Base64 and pasted back into jwt.io. It immediately reported **"signature verification failed"**. A server would reject that token.

**Lesson:** anyone can **read** a JWT payload, so **never put sensitive information in it**. Only include data that is harmless if exposed.

### Problem 1: revocation is hard

- **Sessions:** to log someone out, delete their session row; the next request fails.
- **JWTs:** the token lives on the client, and the server can't make the client delete it. If a user reports "my account is compromised, log me out everywhere", a pure stateless system **can't help**.

Community workarounds:

1. **Blacklisting (denylist)**: store revoked tokens in the database or Redis and reject requests carrying them. (This adds back a server-side lookup.)
2. **Short-lived access tokens + refresh tokens**:
   - On login, issue an **access token** (expires in about **5–10 minutes**) and a **refresh token** (about **1–7 days**, depending on how paranoid you are).
   - Requests carry the access token. When it expires, the server returns **401 Unauthorized**.
   - The client then sends the **refresh token**. If it's valid and not expired, the server issues a **new access token and a new refresh token**, and the cycle continues.
   - A stolen access token works for only a few minutes; a stolen refresh token also expires.

These are workarounds, not perfect solutions.

### Problem 2: where to store the token

- **Local storage**: the most used option, but **readable by any JavaScript**, so XSS can steal it. Not a good choice.
- **HttpOnly cookie**: protected from JavaScript, but now you're back to a cookie-based setup, much like sessions.

### Recommendation

**Prefer stateful, session-based authentication** unless you have specific scaling requirements (e.g. many servers that must each authenticate requests). Even then, you can store sessions in a distributed key–value store like **Redis**. Sessions are **simpler**, revocation is **straightforward**, and they suit most SaaS projects. The trade-offs of stateless auth usually aren't worth it.

If you do use JWTs:

- keep **expiry short**: minutes to hours, not days,
- use **refresh tokens with server-side storage**,
- store tokens in **HttpOnly cookies**, not local storage.

---

## 13. Rate limiting authentication

Without **rate limiting**, an attacker can send thousands or millions of login attempts, trying password after password. Two bad outcomes:

1. they eventually **guess a password** and take over an account,
2. the flood of requests **crashes your server**.

Rate limiting is mandatory for auth endpoints, and useful globally. Be **stricter** on authentication endpoints and more **generous** elsewhere. (Rate limiting with Redis appears in [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/13 Caching/13 Caching#10. Where backends use Redis|lesson 13]].)

### Use several layers

| Layer | Example | Stops | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Per IP** | 10 login attempts per minute per IP | Simple automated attacks | Many users share one IP (offices, universities); attackers rotate IPs with **botnets**, proxy networks or VPNs |
| **Per account** | 5 failures in 15 minutes → lock the account for 24 hours (unless support unlocks it) | Attacks targeting one account, even from rotating IPs | **Password spraying**: trying one common password (e.g. `12345`) once on *many* accounts |
| **Global** | e.g. at most 100 (failed) login attempts per minute across the whole system | Large distributed attacks, including spraying | It's a system-wide signal, so it triggers an alert rather than pinpointing one attacker |

When the global limit trips, you **raise an alert** and respond: block suspicious IPs, show a **CAPTCHA** to separate genuine users from bots, and so on.

The numbers above are examples; tune them to your system.

---

## 14. Authorization vulnerabilities

**Authorization** decides **what an authenticated user is allowed to do**. People rarely confuse the definitions. The problems come from confusing authentication and authorization in the **implementation**.

### The false sense of security

A typical request path (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/10 Controllers, Services, Repositories, Middlewares and Request Context/10 Controllers, Services, Repositories, Middlewares and Request Context|lesson 10]]):

```text
router → (auth middleware) → handler → service → repository → database
```

- A **`requireAuth`**-style middleware sits at the routing layer (skipped for public routes like login). It checks the session cookie or JWT and returns **401/403** if something is wrong.
- Coarse authorization often happens there too: is the user a member, admin or super-admin? Or, more granular, do they have the **`read:books`** permission?

After that, it's tempting to assume the user may access **anything** further down. That assumption is the bug.

### Example

The frontend has a books table with a filter where you can enter book IDs. Entering `5` calls:

```http
GET /books?id=5
```

The request passes authentication and the `read:books` check, then the repository runs:

```sql
SELECT * FROM books WHERE id = 5;
```

But book 5 **belongs to another user**. Having `read:books` doesn't mean you can read **every** book. The query should have been:

```sql
SELECT * FROM books WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2;  -- $2 = user ID from the request context
```

The user ID comes from the **request context**, set by the auth middleware (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/10 Controllers, Services, Repositories, Middlewares and Request Context/10 Controllers, Services, Repositories, Middlewares and Request Context#9. Request context|lesson 10]]).

### Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)

This is **BOLA**: the system checks authentication and authorization at the routing layer but **not at the object (data) level**.

It sounds harmless with books, but a script can **loop over every ID** and download every **invoice** or payment record in the system, or **modify** invoice URLs and account numbers.

**Fix:** carry authorization all the way to the **repository layer**. Don't fetch "invoice 5"; fetch "invoice 5 **that belongs to (or is accessible by) this user**". Do this for **every** query: `SELECT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `INSERT`.

### 404 instead of 403: don't leak existence

A well-meant but leaky pattern:

```js
// ❌ Leaks whether invoice 5 exists
const invoice = await db.findInvoice(5);
if (invoice.userId !== ctx.user.id) return res.status(403).send("Forbidden");
```

**403 Forbidden** is technically correct, but it tells the attacker **"invoice 5 exists, you just can't have it"**. An attacker can **enumerate** IDs (5, 17, 18, …) to map which invoices exist, then plan further attacks such as **social engineering** (tricking people into giving away sensitive details).

Better: put the ownership check **in the query**:

```sql
SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2;
```

No rows → return **404 Not Found**. The attacker can't tell "doesn't exist" from "exists but belongs to someone else".

### Broken Function Level Authorization (BFLA)

Similar, but about **functions**, not data, especially **admin-only** functions.

Example: `GET /admin/invoices` lists **all** invoices for support staff. It **can't** filter by `user_id`, because admins need to see everything (filters like "pending" or "active" are fine).

The mistake is **security through obscurity**: hiding something instead of actually protecting it. The admin panel's URL was never shared, so the developer assumed only admins would find it. But the login flow is the same for members and admins, and there's no role check. Anyone who sees the URL (e.g. by watching network traffic) can log in as a normal user and call the API.

**Fix:** in the routing layer, check the **role** as well as the permission. Both a member and an admin might have `read:invoices`; the difference is the **role** (`member` vs `admin`). Add a **role middleware** that only lets `admin` call admin functions.

### Predictable IDs (IDOR)

Using **sequential IDs** (101, 102, 103) in URLs like `/invoices/102` lets attackers **guess** other records: 101, 103, 109… This enables **enumeration** attacks. The related vulnerability class is **IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference)**.

One mitigation: use **UUIDs** as primary keys, e.g. `3f2b8c1e-9a4d-4e7b-b1c2-7d9e0f6a5b43`. They're random, commonly used as primary keys, and URL-friendly. UUIDs have some **performance trade-offs** worth reading about, but they're generally recommended here. Random IDs **don't replace** ownership checks; they just make guessing harder.

## 15. Horizontal vs vertical attacks, and how to prevent them

Instead of memorising vulnerability names, use two categories:

| Category | What happens | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Horizontal** | User A accesses **user B's resources**: scope widens *across users* | BOLA, IDOR |
| **Vertical** | A user gains **higher privileges**, e.g. reaching admin functions: scope widens *upwards* | BFLA |

### Prevention framework

1. **Centralise authorization logic.** Don't scatter checks across the codebase, where they get applied inconsistently or forgotten. Have one clear authorization layer every request passes through: easy to understand, maintain and scale.
2. **Default deny.** If the authorization logic doesn't **explicitly allow** something, **deny** it. New resources and endpoints are then **protected by default**, even if you forget to configure them.
3. **Test authorization specifically, and automatically.** Don't just test the happy path. Write automated tests (run in your **CI/CD** pipeline) that check:
   - user A **cannot** access user B's resources,
   - a `member` **cannot** call `admin` functions,
   - an unauthenticated user **cannot** reach authenticated resources.

   Manual testing misses cases as the system changes; automated tests keep you as secure as the day you built it.
4. **Audit logs.**
   - Log every access to **sensitive resources** (e.g. admin endpoints): who, what, when.
   - Log every **failed authorization check** (user A trying to read user B's data) as a security event. Someone may be **probing** your system, and you want to know.

## 16. Cross-site scripting (XSS)

**XSS (cross-site scripting)** happens when an attacker gets **their JavaScript to run in another user's browser, in the context of your site**.

### Why it's dangerous

JavaScript running in your site's context can:

- **read everything on the page**, including sensitive data,
- **make API requests as the logged-in user**, using their cookies (unless HttpOnly) and local storage,
- **redirect** the user to **phishing** pages to steal credentials,
- **change the page content** to trick the user.

### Stored XSS: an example

A blogging platform with a **comment board** supporting **Markdown**:

1. The user writes Markdown (`# heading`, `- bullet`).
2. To display it, the app converts it to **HTML** (in React, with libraries like **remark** and **rehype**) and **injects the HTML into the DOM**:

   ```html
   <ul><li>first point</li><li>second point</li></ul>
   ```

3. The HTML is saved on the server and shown to everyone who views the comment.

If an attacker finds a hole in the conversion and slips a `<script>` tag into the HTML, then because the whole HTML is injected into the page, **the script runs for every user who views the comment**. It can send their session cookies and local storage to the attacker's server, hijack sessions, or redirect them to phishing pages.

Popular libraries (remark, rehype, React) handle this safely by default. The risk comes when you build it yourself or work on a **legacy** system.

React deliberately names its raw-HTML prop **`dangerouslySetInnerHTML`**, so you're always warned you're on your own when using it.

### Other kinds

| Type | How the script gets in |
|---|---|
| **Stored XSS** | Saved on the server (e.g. a comment) and served to every viewer |
| **Reflected XSS** | Comes from the request, e.g. the **URL**, and is reflected back into the page |
| **DOM-based XSS** | Frontend code writes untrusted data into the page, e.g. via `innerHTML` |

### Root cause

Same as SQL injection: **user-provided content treated as code instead of data**, only this time in the browser (HTML + JavaScript) instead of the database.

### Prevention

1. **Sanitize** user-provided markup before storing it (in your validation layer): detect and strip dangerous parts such as `<script>` tags, keeping only safe HTML. Use a well-tested sanitizer library rather than writing your own. **Escaping** output by default (as React does) is part of the same idea.
2. **Content Security Policy (CSP).** A **response header** in which the server tells the browser what it may load and run. For example:
   - only run scripts from **specific domains** (your own),
   - **no inline scripts at all**, which would block the injected `<script>` above,
   - only load images from specific domains.

   ```http
   Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; img-src 'self' https://images.example.com
   ```

   *(Illustrative header.)*

**CSP is a last line of defense, not the fix.** The real fix is proper sanitization. CSP is there in case something slips through.

The general rule appears again: **whenever you handle user-provided data** (a search query, HTML, a large image upload), think carefully about how you store it, process it, what access it gets, and what resources you spend on it. That alone avoids the vast majority of vulnerabilities.

## 17. Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)

The creator considers **CSRF** a **minor threat for modern apps** using current libraries and frameworks, though legacy systems and outdated practices still exist.

### How it works

Browsers store cookies per site and **automatically attach them** to requests to that site, **even when the request is triggered from a different site**.

1. You're logged in to `bank.com`; your browser holds its session cookie.
2. You visit `evil.com` (e.g. via a phishing link).
3. `evil.com` contains a form that **auto-submits**, or an image tag or script that triggers a request to `bank.com`.
4. Your browser sends that request **with your bank.com cookie**.
5. `bank.com` sees a valid cookie, treats the request as genuine, and performs the action, e.g. a transfer.

### Why it's mostly handled today

- **SameSite cookies** (section 11): with `Strict`, or `Lax` if your frontend and backend are on different domains, the cookie isn't sent on these cross-site requests. Modern browsers (e.g. Chrome) default to `Lax` when no value is set. Unless you set `SameSite=None`, you're largely protected.
- **CORS** (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/05 HTTP for Backend Engineers/05 HTTP for Backend Engineers#7. CORS and the OPTIONS method|lesson 05]]): the backend only sends CORS headers for its own frontend's origin, so the browser blocks other sites from reading responses and from sending non-simple requests (like JSON `POST`s with custom headers). CORS isn't really a security mechanism and doesn't block simple form submissions, but it's another layer.

## 18. Misconfiguration

Configuration mistakes can open security holes too. (See also [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/17 Configuration Management/17 Configuration Management|lesson 17]].)

### Secrets management

**Secrets** = API keys, database passwords, encryption keys, JWT and other authentication secrets.

- **Never put secrets in source code.** Once committed to git and pushed to GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket, **everyone with repo access** can use them to reach your database, external services and users' data.
- Keep secrets in **environment variables** or a **secrets manager** (AWS Parameter Store, HashiCorp Vault, …).
- **Deleting a leaked secret in a later commit isn't enough.** It's still in the **commit history**. **Rotate** it immediately: revoke it and create a new one.

### Debug mode in production

Locally the log level is usually **debug**, which prints things like:

- detailed errors with **stack traces**, which reveal function names, file names and code structure,
- raw **SQL queries**, database configuration and transaction details,
- sometimes users' sensitive information.

In production the level should be **info**, so none of that is logged. If you forget to configure it, all that detail ends up in production logs, and if those logs are breached, attackers learn a lot about your code, database and users. Know the log level of each environment (local, staging, production). See [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/18 Logging, Monitoring and Observability/18 Logging, Monitoring and Observability#6. Log levels|lesson 18]] and [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/16 Error Handling and Fault-Tolerant Systems/16 Error Handling and Fault-Tolerant Systems#6. Security in error handling|lesson 16]].

### Security headers

Besides **CSP**, other HTTP headers prevent whole classes of attacks. For example:

- **`X-Frame-Options`** stops other sites from embedding your site in an **iframe**. Without it, an attacker can show your real site inside a frame on their page and use **clickjacking** (tricking users into clicking hidden elements) or hidden scripts to capture credentials and interactions.

Almost every web framework has a **security middleware** that sets the industry-standard headers in one line: Express (Node.js), Echo and Gin (Go), Django (Python) and others. Use it rather than configuring each header by hand.

## 19. Boundaries, assumptions and defense in depth

### Everything is about boundaries

Every vulnerability above, and the thousands of others, comes down to **data crossing a boundary**: between systems, privilege levels, languages or markup formats.

| Vulnerability | Boundary crossed |
|---|---|
| SQL injection | Untrusted input → the database query language |
| XSS | User Markdown → HTML/JavaScript in the browser |
| Broken authorization | Requests → data or functions belonging to other users or roles |

Each time you write code, ask:

1. **Where is data crossing a boundary?**
2. **What assumptions am I making about that data?**
3. **What if those assumptions are wrong?**

Asking these consistently avoids the vast majority of vulnerabilities modern backends suffer from.

### Defense in depth

No single defense is perfect, so think in **layers**:

1. **Input validation**: the first line. Strictly validate everything entering the system right after route matching, so data reaching the handler has exactly the expected shape ([[Notes/Backend from First Principles/09 Validations and Transformations/09 Validations and Transformations|lesson 09]]).
2. **Parameterized operations**: parameterized queries for databases, argument lists for OS commands and file operations. No string concatenation.
3. **Authorization at the point of access**: check access where the data is actually read or written (the repository), not a few layers upstream.
4. **Security headers and policies**: CORS, CSP and other headers. Not strong defenses on their own, but they **limit the damage** if something gets through.
5. **Monitoring and logging**: log suspicious activity, send it to your logging service, and raise alerts ([[Notes/Backend from First Principles/18 Logging, Monitoring and Observability/18 Logging, Monitoring and Observability|lesson 18]]).

One layer may have a weakness, but an attacker would have to get past **all of them** at once, which is far less likely.

> Security isn't a feature you learn and implement once. It's a **mindset** you bring to every line of code: always think about **boundaries** and **assumptions**.

## 20. Where to learn more

- **PortSwigger Web Security Academy**: free, from the makers of **Burp Suite** (a well-known penetration testing tool). It covers SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, clickjacking, SSRF, OS command injection, authentication, OAuth and JWT attacks, and more, with theory and **hands-on labs**.
- **OWASP Top 10**: a regularly updated list of the most critical web application security risks from the **OWASP** foundation. **Broken access control** (BOLA, BFLA) tops the current list, which also includes **security misconfiguration** and **injection**.
- **OWASP Cheat Sheet Series**: focused guides per topic, e.g. the **Authentication** and **Session Management** cheat sheets (good and bad practices, why session IDs must come from a CSPRNG, and more).

## Key takeaways

- Attackers look for **assumptions**. Stop assuming input is clean, users are who they claim, or requests come from your frontend.
- **Injection** = data treated as code. Fix with **parameterized queries** and **argument arrays**; never concatenate user input into SQL, shell or HTML.
- Give the app's database user **DML-only** permissions.
- Consider an **auth provider**, but understand authentication anyway.
- Passwords: **never plain text**; use a **slow, salted** hash (**Argon2id** or bcrypt), not MD5 or SHA-256.
- Session IDs: long, **CSPRNG**-generated. Cookies: **HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict/Lax**.
- JWT payloads are **readable**; revocation is hard. **Prefer stateful sessions**; if you use JWTs, keep them short-lived with refresh tokens in HttpOnly cookies.
- **Layered rate limiting** on auth: per IP, per account, global.
- Check authorization **at the point of access** (in the query). Return **404** instead of 403 to avoid leaking existence. Check **roles** for admin functions. Avoid predictable IDs.
- **Centralise** authorization, **default deny**, **automate** authorization tests, keep **audit logs**.
- **XSS**: sanitize user content; **CSP** is the last line of defense, not the fix.
- **CSRF** is largely handled by SameSite cookies (plus CORS).
- Avoid **misconfiguration**: no secrets in git (rotate if leaked), no debug logs in production, use a security-headers middleware.
- Think in **boundaries** and **layers**.
